name: Margu
confidence_why: Capell 1942, the only first-hand description of Margu (Croker Island), reports that the tonic accent is irregular and states no rule, and the sole contrary placement, an initial-stress listing for Marrgu in Goedemans 1998, cites no source and is marked by its author as having many exceptions and needing caution.
catalog_citation: Capell, A. 1942. Languages of Arnhem Land, North Australia (continued). Oceania 13(1): 24-50. Section (24) Margu, pp. 34-35; comparative vocabulary p. 39.
catalog_locator: p. 34, section (24) Margu, first paragraph (PDF page 34 of the archive.org scan sim_oceania_1942-09_13_1; file the copy we hold; pages 34 and 39 rendered at 150 dpi and read by the third reader)
catalog_quote: (24) Margu. This was the language of Croker Island, but it is doubtful whether half a dozen speakers still exist. Most of the information was obtained from an old native named Ormu, now reputed “ king ” of Croker Island, and two younger men, half Iwaidja, half Margu, from the mainland, by the medium partly of pidgin English and partly of Iwaidja. The phonetics of Margu are difficult, especially the frequent occurrence of γ and the irregularity of the tonic accent. I have written the bilabial v in some instances, but it is not always easy to distinguish from w, e.g. vaγin, son or daughter. The mixed vowel ï is also of very frequent occurrence. Consonantal endings are practically the normal use.
world_status: statement found in an open source

PDF page 34 = journal p. 34; I rendered the page image at 150 dpi and read it directly. The quoted passage is there verbatim, section '(24) Margu.': '..The phonetics of Margu are difficult, especially the frequent occurrence of γ and the irregularity of the tonic accent. I have written the bilabial v in some instances, but it is not always easy to distinguish from w, e.g. vaγin, son or daughter. The mixed vowel ï is also of very frequent occurrence. Consonantal endings are practically the normal use.' The reader's quote correctly restores γ and ï where the text layer has 'y'/'j'; every word matches the image. I…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Capell, the only first-hand describer to comment, found word accent ('tonic accent') irregular, i.e. not falling on a predictable syllable; he states no rule. The only positional claim anywhere is second-hand: Goedemans (1998: 238) files Marrgu under initial main stress but flags it (E) 'many exceptions' and 'No reference' (deduced from scanty archival material, 'handle with caution'). Net: accent position not established; weak evidence for initial-with-many-exceptions or lexically variable accent.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing first-hand. Goedemans's category I implies alternating secondary stress by category definition only, not from a Marrgu source.
new_statements.exceptions: Capell: accent 'irregular' (no examples with accent marks in the published sketch). Goedemans: code E = many exceptions to initial stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Capell's remark concerns word-level phonetics of elicited citation forms obtained through pidgin English and Iwaidja from one old speaker and two semi-speakers; no phrase-level discussion.
new_statements.identity_note: Capell 1942 writes 'Margu' (Croker Island language) = Glottolog marg1251 Margu / Marrku / Marrgu (ISO mhg), Tindale T107; data from one elderly Croker Island speaker (Ormu) and two Iwaidja-Margu semi-speakers, elicited via pidgin English and Iwaidja, so Iwaidja colouring is possible (Capell himself notes this for the possessive prefixes). Goedemans 1998 'Marrgu (T107)' is the same language. Note the Glottolog 'glottolog_refs' list supplied in our source list for this key is spurious (unrelated works matched on 'Marg'); the real Glottolog bibliography (23 items) was downloaded via langdoc complexquery and contains no grammar or phonology of Margu.
